minor: 'Djibouti ... still holds the southern shore' and 'France held the southern shore' follow the source wording, but Djibouti sits on the African (western) side of the strait. 'Southern coast of the strait's African shore' or similar would be clearer.
'saving about 6,500 kilometres' uses the difference of the two rounded legs (21,800 - 15,300). The table difference is about 6,420 km, so 'about 6,400' would be exact; 'about 6,500' is acceptable.
'three European empires took its shores': Italy in 1869 was a kingdom with no empire yet. 'Three European powers' is safer.
'In 2024, that detour meant more days at sea and more fuel burned' has no figure and no source entry. It is a safe general claim, but add a source or a number such as extra days.
'Qatar mediated, then withdrew its peacekeepers in 2017': the 2010 mediation is not in the listed sources, though it is documented.
'so its troubles reach your shop shelves' is a general causal claim with no source entry. It is fair as framing, but soften it or source it.

shots.vo: The Red Sea runs about 1,930 kilometres, from Egypt's Suez in the north to this gate in the south.
At its top is the Suez Canal, opened in 1869, the shortcut between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean.
At its bottom, the sea narrows between Yemen on the Arabian side and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African side.
Any ship sailing from Suez to the Indian Ocean has no other way out of the Red Sea.

map.label: Suez to the Indian Ocean: the only way out of the Red Sea

shots.vo: How wide is the gap? The US Energy Information Administration says about 29 kilometres; Britannica says about 32.
An island called Perim splits it into a shallow eastern channel, about 3 kilometres wide, and a western one about 26.
Perim belongs to Yemen, and it is only about 13 square kilometres of dry, rocky land.
Big ships use the deep western channel, in two traffic lanes, one for each direction, separated by a buffer.
In 2023, Egypt's canal authority counted about 26,400 ships through Suez, more than 70 every day.

shots.vo: On the Arabian shore is Yemen, divided by civil war since 2014, when a northern movement, the Houthis, took the capital.
Forces allied with Yemen's internationally recognised government hold the coast right beside the strait, including the town of Mocha.
Further north, the Houthis hold the capital, Sanaa, and the Red Sea port of Hodeidah.
Tankers from the Gulf heading to Europe, and container ships from China, funnel through this one door.
So how did one small gate end up with so many flags along its shores?

shots.vo: In January 1839, British forces captured Aden, a harbour about 170 kilometres east of the strait.
Britain wanted a coaling station there for the steamships sailing between Britain and India.

shots.vo: Britain now held a port on the Arabian shore, beside the sea road to India.
In 1857, Britain also took Perim, the island sitting in the middle of the strait itself.
In 1862, France signed a treaty with local Afar rulers for Obock, on the African shore facing the strait.
In 1869, the year the Suez Canal opened, an Italian shipping company bought land at Assab, further north.
The canal put this strait on the main sea road between Europe and Asia, and three European empires took its shores.
By 1890, France held the southern shore, Italy held Eritrea to the north, and Britain held Aden opposite.
Those colonial lines outlived the empires; Britain left Aden in November 1967, and Perim went to the new South Yemen.
In June 1977, France's last territory here became independent Djibouti, which still holds the southern shore.
In 1993, Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia, and Ethiopia was left without any coast of its own.
Ethiopia now has about 130 million people, making it the most populous landlocked country in the world.

shots.vo: In December 1995, Eritrea and Yemen fought a short war over the Hanish Islands, north of the strait.
In 1998, an arbitration tribunal awarded most of the islands to Yemen, and both countries accepted the ruling.

document.title: Eritrea–Yemen Arbitration, Award on Territorial Sovereignty, 9 October 1998
document.highlight: The islands of the Zuqar-Hanish group are subject to the territorial sovereignty of Yemen.

shots.prompt: Map action: painted map of the southern Red Sea, the Hanish Islands shown first in neutral grey, then changing colour to Yemen's colour as the ruling lands.

shots.vo: A second award in 1999 drew the sea border between the two countries roughly down the middle of the Red Sea.
Not every line is settled: Djibouti and Eritrea both claim Ras Doumeira, a headland on their border near the strait's western approach.
Their troops clashed there in June 2008; Qatar mediated, then withdrew its peacekeepers in 2017.
Ras Doumeira is still disputed, and the border there is still unmarked on the map.
By then, every shore had a flag, and soon those shores filled with foreign military bases.
Djibouti has about a million people, yet it hosts bases of the United States, France, China, Japan and Italy.
Under a 2014 deal, the United States pays about 63 million dollars a year for Camp Lemonnier.

shots.vo: In August 2017, China opened its first overseas military base here, about 12 kilometres from the American camp.
The gate has been shut before: in October 1973, at war with Israel, Egypt's navy blockaded it.
The strait was shut to Israel-bound ships, though no border moved.
About fifty years later, on 19 November 2023, Houthi forces seized a car carrier, the Galaxy Leader, in the southern Red Sea.
The Houthis said they acted over Israel's war in Gaza, about 2,000 kilometres away.
They said they targeted ships linked to Israel, and later added ships they linked to the United States and Britain.

shots.vo: Many big shipping lines answered by sending their ships the long way, around Africa's Cape of Good Hope.
From Singapore to Rotterdam, that means about 21,800 kilometres at sea instead of about 15,300 through Suez.
Egypt's canal authority says Suez traffic fell from about 26,400 ships in 2023 to about 13,200 in 2024.

shots.vo: In December 2024, Egypt's president said the canal had lost almost seven billion dollars that year.
The EIA says oil through the strait fell from 8.7 to about 4 million barrels a day in 2024.
In December 2023, the United States launched a naval coalition to protect ships, calling it a defence of free navigation.
From January 2024, US and British forces struck Houthi targets inside Yemen, and in February the EU began escorting ships.
The Houthis say they are acting in solidarity with Gaza, and will stop when the war there does.
They point to their pause in attacks during the January 2025 Gaza ceasefire.
In January 2024, the UN Security Council demanded that the Houthis stop all attacks on merchant ships.

document.highlight: Demands that the Houthis immediately cease all attacks against merchant and commercial vessels.

In May 2025, Oman announced a truce between the United States and the Houthis; the Houthis said Israel was not included.
In July 2025, two more cargo ships, the Magic Seas and the Eternity C, were sunk off Yemen.
After the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, attacks largely paused, but big shipping lines said any return would be gradual.
So will the gate stay open, and what happens to the map if it does not?
Road one: calm holds, and the shortcut wins again, saving about 6,500 kilometres on a Singapore to Rotterdam run.
In 2023, before the crisis, the canal earned a record 10.25 billion dollars, Egypt's canal authority says.

In 2024, that detour meant more days at sea and more fuel burned on every Asia–Europe trip.

shots.vo: Ethiopia says it needs sea access, and in January 2024 it signed a deal with Somaliland for a stretch of coast.
Somalia, which counts Somaliland as its own territory, called the deal a breach of its sovereignty.
In December 2024, after talks brokered by Turkey in Ankara, Ethiopia and Somalia agreed a path to settle the dispute.
Eritrea's port of Assab lies less than 100 kilometres from Ethiopia's border; Eritrea says it will not discuss its coast.
Every one of these roads still begins, or ends, at the same narrow stretch of water.

shots.vo: The strait never got any narrower; what turned the ships away was the attacks launched from Yemen.
Next, we go east, to Malacca: the narrow lane past Singapore that much of Asia's oil must squeeze through.
